title: A Fire in My Bones: Jeremiah in the Stocks
summary: Pashhur, the priest in charge of the temple, has Jeremiah beaten and locked overnight in the stocks. On his release Jeremiah renames him Terror on Every Side and announces the exile to Babylon by name for the first time. Then comes the most raw of Jeremiah's confessions: he accuses God of overpowering him, says the word burns like fire in his bones when he tries to keep silent, breaks into praise, and finally curses the day he was born.
story: Chapter 19 ended with Jeremiah preaching in the temple courtyard. Chapter 20 shows the cost. For the first time the book narrates physical violence against the prophet, and for the first time it names Babylon as the enemy from the north (verse 4). The chapter closes the long section that began in chapter 11, and it closes it with the last and darkest of the confessions. After this, the book changes character: chapter 21 jumps forward to the final siege under Zedekiah, and the personal laments do not return. It is as if the prophet's inner struggle has been laid bare once, fully, and then he simply keeps going.
historical:
Pashhur son of Immer belonged to the priestly clan of Immer, one of the priestly families listed in 1 Chronicles 24:14 and among the returned exiles in Ezra 2:37. He is described as “the chief official in the house of the LORD”, responsible for order in the temple, which gave him authority to punish a prophet he considered a disturber of the peace (compare 29:26, where such an official is expected to put madmen who prophesy in the stocks). He is a different man from Pashhur son of Malchijah in 21:1. Verse 6 says he had “prophesied these lies”, which suggests he also spoke as a prophet, assuring people that Jerusalem was safe.

The Upper Gate of Benjamin was probably a gate of the temple complex on its north side, facing the territory of Benjamin. This is the first time the book names Babylon as the destroyer. The chapter probably belongs to the reign of Jehoiakim, around 605 BC or after, when Nebuchadnezzar's victory over Egypt at Carchemish (605 BC) made it clear which empire would dominate the region. Pashhur's own fate, deportation to Babylon, fits the deportations of 597 BC.
cultural:
The stocks (verse 2) translate a word related to twisting or turning, suggesting a wooden frame that held the feet, hands, and perhaps neck in a painful, bent position. Being held there at a temple gate meant public humiliation as well as pain. Renaming someone was a powerful act in the ancient world. Names carried meaning, and a prophet who gave a new name was announcing a new destiny. “Magor-missabib”, Terror on Every Side, is a phrase Jeremiah uses repeatedly (6:25; 46:5; 49:29), and here it becomes the priest's identity: the man who promised safety will himself embody fear.

In verse 15 the birth of a son is announced to his father by a messenger, a moment of great joy in a culture where sons carried on the family name and land. Jeremiah's curse on that messenger is not an attack on a real person but a poetic way of wishing his own existence undone. The “cities that the LORD overthrew without compassion” (verse 16) are Sodom and Gomorrah, proverbial for total destruction. Cursing the day of one's birth was a recognized form of lament; Job opens his speeches with an extended version (Job 3).
literary: The chapter has a narrative (verses 1 to 6) and two poems. The narrative ends with Jeremiah's oracle against Pashhur. Verses 7 to 13 are a lament that moves through the classic stages of the lament psalms: complaint (verses 7 and 8), description of inner struggle (verse 9) and of enemies (verse 10), confession of trust (verse 11), plea (verse 12), and praise (verse 13). Its key verbs are chosen with care: “deceived” and “prevailed” appear first in Jeremiah's accusation against God and then in his enemies' mouths (“Perhaps he will be deceived so that we may prevail against him”), and finally God is the warrior against whom persecutors “will not prevail”. Then, without transition, verses 14 to 18 plunge from praise into a curse on the day of his birth. Some scholars think the two poems were placed side by side deliberately to show how faith and despair can sit together in one person; others think the sequence is an editor's arrangement. Either way, the book lets the darkness have the last word in this section.

outline.t: Pashhur beats Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks
Terror on Every Side: the exile to Babylon named
You deceived me, and the fire in my bones
The LORD is with me like a fearsome warrior
Cursed be the day I was born

doctrines.note: Jeremiah suffers because he is faithful, and Scripture records his agony without editing it into piety. The chapter shows that deep anguish is not proof of weak faith; the man who cursed his birthday is the same man who kept preaching.
God's word is not a message Jeremiah controls. When he tries to keep silent it becomes “a fire burning in my heart”. The prophet is held by the word as much as he holds it.

Everything in the chapter, accusation, praise, and the wish never to have been born, is spoken to God or before God. Jeremiah's prayer teaches that no feeling is too dark to bring into God's presence.

words.note: Patah, to entice, persuade, or deceive. It can describe seducing a young woman (Exodus 22:16) or luring someone into a trap (1 Kings 22:20-22). “You have deceived me, O LORD” is a shocking thing to say. Interpreters render it variously as deceived, enticed, or persuaded: Jeremiah may mean that God lured him into a calling whose cost he could not have known, or overpowered him when he was young (1:6-7). The same verb returns in verse 10 on the lips of his enemies.

Magor-missabib, Terror on Every Side, the new name Jeremiah gives Pashhur. The phrase appears several times in Jeremiah and also in Psalm 31:13. In verse 10 it seems his enemies mockingly used it as a nickname for Jeremiah himself, turning his own words against him.

Esh, fire. In verse 9 God's word is like “a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones”. Elsewhere God tells Jeremiah that his words in the prophet's mouth will be fire (5:14; 23:29). The image captures both the power of the word and the pain of carrying it: fire gives light and heat, but it also consumes.

christ: Jeremiah, beaten by the temple authorities, mocked all day, and watched by friends waiting for him to fall, walks a path that Jesus walked more fully: struck at the high priest's house, mocked, and betrayed by a friend (Mark 14:65; 15:16-20). The resemblance is a pattern, not a prediction. The lament of verses 7 to 13 moves from agony to praise, much as Psalm 22 does, the psalm Jesus prayed from the cross (Mark 15:34). And the darkness of verses 14 to 18 is not the end of the story. The New Testament proclaims a Savior who entered the deepest human anguish, who in Gethsemane said his soul was sorrowful to the point of death (Mark 14:34), and who did not despise such sorrow but bore it. Hebrews says that because he suffered he is able to help those who are tested (Hebrews 2:18).

hard.q: How can a prophet of God curse the day he was born, and what does this passage offer someone who feels the same way?
hard.a:
Verses 14 to 18 are among the darkest words in the Bible, and they sit in Scripture unexplained and uncorrected. Jeremiah does not ask to die, and he does not harm himself; he cries out that he wishes he had never been born, because his life has been filled with “trouble and sorrow” and, he fears, will end in shame. Job says much the same (Job 3), and so, in different ways, do Moses (Numbers 11:15) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:4). In the stories of Moses and Elijah, God answers with help, food, and rest rather than condemnation (Numbers 11:16-17; 1 Kings 19:5-8). The Bible does not treat such words as a failure of faith or diagnose the person who speaks them. It treats them as prayer: speech addressed to God by someone who is still, even here, talking to him. It is worth noticing that Jeremiah's story did not end in this chapter. He lived on through siege and exile, and his book goes on to contain some of Scripture's greatest words of hope (29:11; 31:31-34).

If you are reading this passage because you share Jeremiah's wish, please don't carry it alone. Tell someone you trust today: a friend, a family member, a pastor, a doctor. If you are thinking about ending your life or are in danger, reach out now to emergency services where you live; in the United States you can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any hour. Jeremiah brought his darkness into the open before God. You are allowed to bring yours into the open too, before God and before people who can help you.

questions: Jeremiah said God's word was like a fire he couldn't hold in. Is there a truth or a calling you have tried to keep silent about? What happens when you do?
The lament of verses 7 to 13 moves from accusation to praise, and then verses 14 to 18 fall back into darkness. What does it mean to you that the Bible doesn't tidy up that sequence?
Who are the people you would tell if you were in a season as dark as Jeremiah's? If there is no one, what is one step you could take toward someone who could walk with you?
